442.title: Or — a luminous object; or a sorrowless mind; or a great heart (1.35–1.39)
442.hook: five more 'or's, ending with the most generous line in the Yoga Sutras: whatever you find dear
442.tomorrow: mastery from the smallest to the largest
442.howItsDone: Hindu meditators use many supports, from an inner light in the heart to the image of a saint or a chosen form of God, and teachers often cite sutra 1.39 to encourage each student to meditate on what is dear to them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: or the breath. A long breath out, a small rest at the bottom. Did you use that door once? Today Patanjali keeps opening doors, five in a row. Day four hundred forty-two.
screen: `OR THE BREATH — A LONG BREATH OUT.`

segments.voice: A big old house has a front door, a back door, a side gate, a door from the garage, and a window someone always climbs through. Everyone in the family gets in a different way, and nobody argues about which door is the real one. They just want to get home. In sutras 1.35 to 1.39, Patanjali turns into that kind of house. One after another, five more sutras begin with the same word: or.
screen: `A HOUSE WITH MANY DOORS.` → `NOBODY ARGUES WHICH IS REAL.` → `FIVE MORE SUTRAS: OR.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.35: or, when a subtle sense experience arises, it holds the mind steady. The commentator Vyasa gives an example: resting attention on the tip of the nose, a practitioner may sense an unusually fine fragrance. The point isn't the fragrance; it's that a vivid, fine sensation can anchor a wandering mind. Sutra 1.36: or, the sorrowless, luminous one. Vyasa places it in the heart, an inner light without grief. Some teachers picture a soft light in the chest. Sutra 1.37: or, a mind that takes as its object someone free of attachment. A great heart, a saint, a teacher: Vyasa says a mind colored by one free of passion finds its footing. Sutra 1.38: or, resting on what's known in dream or in deep sleep: the stillness of dreamless sleep, or an inspiring dream, as a support. And then sutra 1.39, short and wide open: or, by meditating on whatever you find dear. Whatever appeals to you. After all the talk of effort, the list ends by leaving the choice to the practitioner. Not because anything goes. Vyasa explains: once the mind finds its footing on what it likes, it can find its footing elsewhere too. Notice the whole sweep, from 1.33 to 1.39: four attitudes, the breath, a fine sensation, an inner light, a great heart, dream and sleep, anything dear. Many doors. One house.
screen: `A FINE SENSATION; AN INNER LIGHT.` · `A GREAT HEART TO REST ON.` · `DREAM AND DEEP SLEEP.` · then, large: `OR: WHATEVER YOU FIND DEAR.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Today, you choose the door. Maybe a soft light in the chest. Maybe the face of someone whose goodness you trust, a grandparent, a teacher, a saint. Maybe an image you simply love: the sea, a flame, a tree. If you pray, it may be a form of God dear to you. Choose one, and rest your attention there. When the mind wanders, come back through the same door. The bell holds the time.
Or. Five more times in sutras 1.35 to 1.39: a fine sensation, an inner light, a great heart, dream and sleep, and whatever you find dear.
Your line: many doors. Today, notice what naturally steadies you, a song, a face, a view, and let it be your door for one quiet minute. Day four hundred forty-two.

443.title: Mastery from the smallest to the largest (1.40)
443.hook: a mind steadied through any of the doors can rest on anything, from a speck to the sky
443.howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras treat 1.40 as the sign that the mind has been steadied, and teachers then move to the crystal image of 1.41 to describe what deeper absorption is like.

segments.voice: Yesterday: many doors. A fine sensation, an inner light, a great heart, dream and sleep, and whatever you find dear. Which door did you use? Today, what's waiting once you're through. Day four hundred forty-three.

A good photographer can focus on a grain of pollen on a bee's leg, then, without changing cameras, pull back and frame a mountain range at dusk. What matters isn't the size of the thing. It's that the lens holds steady on whatever it's pointed at. Patanjali has spent seven sutras offering doors into a steady mind. Sutra 1.40 says what a mind like that can hold, at both ends of the scale.
screen: `POLLEN ON A BEE'S LEG.` → `A MOUNTAIN RANGE AT DUSK.` → `ONE STEADY LENS.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.40, in paraphrase: the yogi's mastery extends from the smallest particle to the greatest magnitude. Paramanu, the smallest atom. Parama mahat, the greatest greatness. Vashikara, mastery, having it under one's control. What kind of mastery? The commentator Vyasa explains that the mind can now settle on the subtlest object without slipping, and on the vastest object without losing its grip. Small doesn't make it fidget. Huge doesn't make it scatter. This might remind you of the Shvetashvatara, a little over two weeks ago: smaller than small, greater than great. There the words described the self. Here they describe the reach of a steadied mind. And notice what this sutra is doing in the book. It's a hinge. The long list of doors is finished. From here, Patanjali moves on to describe what happens inside absorption itself. The next sutra brings one more image, a mind like a clear crystal, and that's where today's carry comes from. Tomorrow unfolds it. For today, the direction is enough: a mind that has been steadied through any door becomes clear enough to hold anything, from a speck of dust to the whole sky.
screen: `PARAMANU TO PARAMA MAHAT.` · `SMALL DOESN'T MAKE IT FIDGET.` · `AN ECHO OF THE SHVETASHVATARA.` · then, large: `A MIND LIKE A CLEAR CRYSTAL.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. First, rest attention on the smallest thing you can feel: one point of contact, the tip of a finger on your knee. Hold it gently. Then widen to the whole body sitting. Then the whole room. Then imagine the sky above the roof. Then come back to the fingertip. Small, then large, then small. The aim isn't to see far. It's to notice whether the steadiness holds as the size changes. The bell holds the time.
Vashikara, mastery, having it under control. Sutra 1.40: a steadied mind can rest on anything, from the tiniest particle to the greatest expanse.

Your line: the clear crystal. Today, give one small thing and one big thing your full, steady attention: a cup of tea, then the evening sky. Notice whether you can stay clear for both. Day four hundred forty-three.

444.title: The stages of absorption (1.41–1.46)
444.hook: a clear crystal on a red cloth looks red; Patanjali says a still mind behaves the same way
444.howItsDone: Teachers of classical yoga describe samapatti as the mind becoming transparent to its object, and they guide students from coarse objects, such as an image or the breath, toward subtler ones over long practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mastery from the smallest to the largest, vashikara, and a promise: the clear crystal. Did the tea and the sky both get your full attention? Today the crystal itself. Day four hundred forty-four.

Put a clear glass bead on a red cloth. It looks red. Slide it onto blue silk. It looks blue. Set it on a leaf, and it glows green. The bead hasn't changed at all. It has no color of its own, and that's exactly why it can show every color perfectly. Most of the time our minds aren't like that. They're tinted glass: everything we look at comes back colored with our worry, our wanting, our labels. Sutra 1.41 describes the moment the tint drains away.
screen: `A CLEAR BEAD ON RED CLOTH.` → `ON BLUE SILK. ON A LEAF.` → `NO COLOR OF ITS OWN.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.41, in paraphrase: when the turnings have dwindled, the mind becomes like a fine, transparent jewel, and takes on the form of whatever it rests on, whether the knower, the act of knowing, or the thing known. That merging is called samapatti, coinciding. The crystal takes the color. Then Patanjali lays out the stages. First, savitarka, absorption on a coarse object, still mixed with three things: the word, the object, and the idea of it. Vyasa's example is a cow: the sound cow, the animal, and the thought of a cow, all tangled together. Next, nirvitarka. Memory is cleaned out, the mind becomes as if empty of its own form, and only the object shines. Not the label cow. Just the cow, seen. Sutra 1.44 says the same two steps happen with subtle objects: savichara, still with some thinking, and nirvichara, without it. Sutra 1.45 says subtle objects go all the way back to the unmanifest, the root of nature itself. And sutra 1.46 gathers the whole set: these are samadhi with seed. You met that phrase ten days ago. Now you know what the seeds are: every object, coarse or subtle, that the clear mind still rests on. Notice how practical the first step is. Most of the time we don't see things; we see their names. The crystal begins when the name drops away for a moment, and the thing itself is simply there.
screen: `THE MIND LIKE A TRANSPARENT JEWEL.` · `SAVITARKA: WORD, THING, IDEA.` · `NIRVITARKA: ONLY THE OBJECT SHINES.` · then, large: `ALL OF THESE: WITH SEED.`

segments.voice: Before you close your eyes, pick an object near you: a cup, a plant, your own hand. Look at it. Notice the name arrive: cup. Notice ideas follow: mine, chipped, needs washing. Now, gently, let the name and ideas go, and just look. Shape, light, color. If the label comes back, let it pass. Then close your eyes and keep the object in mind, without words, like the crystal on the cloth. The bell holds the time.
Samapatti, coinciding, the mind taking the form of what it rests on. The stages move from thought to without, on coarse objects and on subtle ones, the steps of samadhi with seed.
Your line: the crystal takes the color. Once today, look at something ordinary for ten seconds without naming it, and let it show you its own color. Day four hundred forty-four.

445.title: Truth-bearing wisdom (1.47–1.50)
445.hook: at the clearest stage of absorption, Patanjali says a different kind of knowing appears, and gives it an old Vedic name
445.howItsDone: In classical yoga, ritambhara prajna is described as the fruit of mature absorption, and teachers often contrast it with book learning and reasoning, both valued as steps along the way.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samapatti, the crystal takes the color. With labels, then without; coarse objects, then subtle ones. Did you look at something without naming it? Today, what the clearest crystal knows. Day four hundred forty-five.

There are two ways to know your grandmother's kitchen. You can read a description of it: yellow walls, a table by the window, a smell of cardamom. Or you can stand in it. Both are real knowledge. But only one of them knows this kitchen, this light on this afternoon, this exact chipped cup. Patanjali says that at the clearest stage of absorption, the mind stops knowing about things and starts knowing them, one by one, as they are.
screen: `A DESCRIPTION OF THE KITCHEN.` → `STANDING IN IT.` → `KNOWING ABOUT, AND KNOWING.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.47: when nirvichara, the subtle absorption without thinking, becomes fully clear and skillful, there is inner serenity. Adhyatma prasada, the self made calm and bright. Sutra 1.48: there, wisdom is ritambhara. Truth-bearing. Ritam is a very old word. In the Rig Veda, rita is the cosmic order, the rightness that makes the sun rise and the seasons turn, closely tied to truth itself. Bhara means bearing, carrying, full of. So ritambhara is wisdom that carries the truth in it, wisdom that can't be mistaken, because nothing of the mind's own color has been added. Sutra 1.49 says how it differs from ordinary knowledge. What we learn by testimony, from a teacher or a book, and what we learn by inference, reasoning it out, are about things in general. Truth-bearing wisdom has a different object: the particular. Not what kitchens are like. This kitchen. Not what a self is. This one, here. And sutra 1.50 adds something subtle. Every experience leaves an impression, a samskara, a groove in the mind. The impression left by this wisdom is so strong that it blocks the others. It's like a deep, clean groove that the water now runs in, so the old ruts dry up. That's why, for Patanjali, this isn't the end yet. There's still one impression left: this wisdom's own. And tomorrow, he says what happens when even that is let go.
screen: `ADHYATMA PRASADA: INNER SERENITY.` · `RITAM: THE COSMIC ORDER, TRUTH.` · `NOT KNOWING ABOUT: KNOWING THIS.` · then, large: `A GROOVE THAT BLOCKS THE OTHERS.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Choose one simple thing to know directly, right now: the sensation in the palms of your hands. Not what hands are. Not a memory of your hands. These sensations, here: warmth, tingling, pressure, pulse. Let the mind rest there without commentary, the way the clear crystal rests on its cloth. Each time a thought about the hands arrives, return to the hands themselves. The bell holds the time.
Truth-bearing wisdom. Ritambhara prajna, sutra 1.48: the knowing that arises in the clearest absorption, full of truth, and aimed at the particular, as it is.
Your line: ritambhara. Today, choose one person or thing you think you know all about, and spend one minute just meeting it, this one, here, as if for the first time. Day four hundred forty-five.

446.title: Seedless (1.51)
446.hook: the first chapter of the Yoga Sutras ends by letting go of the very last thing the mind holds
446.howItsDone: In classical yoga, seedless samadhi is described as the culmination of practice, and students study the whole first chapter as a map from the definition of yoga in 1.2 to its completion in 1.51.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ritambhara, truth-bearing wisdom, the knowing that carries the truth and leaves a groove that blocks all the others. Did you meet one thing as if for the first time? Today, the last sutra of chapter one. Day four hundred forty-six.

A gardener clears a field. First the big weeds. Then the small ones. Then the seeds still lying in the soil, waiting to sprout. At last there's one seed left: the special one she planted on purpose, the one that crowded out all the weeds. The field is quiet and clean. And now, strangely, she lets that one go too. Not because it was bad. Because the field was the point all along. That's sutra 1.51, the last line of the first chapter.
screen: `THE BIG WEEDS, THE SMALL ONES.` → `ONE GOOD SEED LEFT.` → `SHE LETS THAT ONE GO TOO.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.51: tasyapi nirodhe sarva nirodhan nirbijah samadhih. When even that is stilled, everything being stilled, there is seedless absorption. Even that: the impression left by yesterday's truth-bearing wisdom, the last good groove in the mind. When it too goes quiet, there's nothing left that could sprout again. Nirbija: without seed. Vyasa explains that the mind then dissolves back into its source, and the seer, purusha, rests alone, pure and free. And that loops all the way back to the third sutra, fifteen days ago: then the seer rests in its own form. The first chapter is a circle. It began with the definition of yoga, and it ends with yoga complete. Look at the path the chapter walked. Atha, now. The seer. The five turnings. Practice and non-attachment. Samadhi with seed, and without. The born-free and the rest of us. Or, devotion to Ishvara. Om, repeated with its meaning. The nine obstacles. One thing. The four keys. Or the breath. Many doors. Mastery, small to large. The crystal taking the color. Truth-bearing wisdom. And seedless. Seventeen sessions, from now to nothing held. This chapter is called the Samadhi Pada, the part on absorption. Tomorrow begins the Sadhana Pada, the part on practice, and it starts with three simple things.
screen: `EVEN THAT IS STILLED.` · `NIRBIJA: NOTHING LEFT TO SPROUT.` · `BACK TO 1.3: THE SEER RESTS.` · `SEVENTEEN SESSIONS, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `SEEDLESS.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Choose one simple support, the breath, and rest on it for a while. Then, without forcing anything, loosen your grip on the breath too. Let it breathe itself, and don't hold on to it as an object. Just sit, holding nothing in particular, aware. If a thought comes, it's fine; let it go without picking up a new support. This isn't about reaching anything. It's a taste of letting go of even the good seed. The bell holds the time.
Seedless. Nirbija samadhi, sutra 1.51: when even the last good impression is stilled, nothing remains that could sprout, and the seer rests in itself.
Your line: nirbija. Today, after you finish something you did well, let it go completely, no replaying, no polishing, and notice the quiet that's left. Day four hundred forty-six.

screen: `DAY 446 COUNTS.` → `SAMADHI PADA, DONE.` → `TOMORROW: KRIYA YOGA — DISCIPLINE, STUDY, SURRENDER.`

447.title: Kriya yoga — discipline, study, surrender (2.1–2.2)
447.hook: the second chapter of the Yoga Sutras opens for busy, scattered minds with a three-part yoga of action
447.howItsDone: Some Hindus who follow the Yoga Sutras practice kriya yoga as a daily rhythm: a disciplined habit such as early rising or fasting, regular study of scripture or mantra repetition, and offering the day's actions to God.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nirbija, seedless, the end of the first chapter, where even the last good seed is let go. Did you let something finished stay finished? Today, chapter two begins. Day four hundred forty-seven.

Chapter one was beautiful. Stilling the mind, the clear crystal, seedless absorption. It can also sound like a story about astronauts: wonderful, and a long way from a life with a job, a family, a phone that buzzes and a mind with forty tabs open. The commentator Vyasa seems to have expected that. He says the first chapter speaks to a mind already settled. The second chapter, he says, is for a mind that is still scattered. And it opens with something you can do this afternoon.
screen: `CHAPTER ONE: THE ASTRONAUTS.` → `A MIND WITH FORTY TABS.` → `CHAPTER TWO: FOR THE REST OF US.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.1: tapah svadhyaya ishvara pranidhanani kriya yogah. Discipline, study and surrender to the Lord are the yoga of action. Kriya means action, doing. So this is yoga you do, in daily life, before the deep stillness comes. Three parts. Tapas, discipline. The word literally means heat, the warmth of effort. Vyasa insists it shouldn't wreck your health; it's the steady heat of keeping your commitments when comfort pulls the other way. Svadhyaya, study. Literally one's own reading: study of the sacred texts, and Vyasa adds repetition of om or a mantra. Some modern teachers also hear in it study of oneself. Ishvara pranidhana, surrender to the Lord, which you met in chapter one as a shortcut. Here Vyasa reads it as offering all your actions to the Lord, the supreme teacher, and letting go of their fruits. Then sutra 2.2 says why: for cultivating samadhi, and for thinning the afflictions. Thinning is the key word. Not destroying them in one blow. Wearing them down, the way water wears down stone. Notice the balance of the three. Discipline is effort. Study is understanding. Surrender is letting go. Body, mind, heart. If you only had discipline, you'd become rigid. Only study, and you'd become clever. Only surrender, and you might drift. Together they make a practice an ordinary person can live. And the same three will return later in this chapter, as the last three of the five observances.
screen: `KRIYA: YOGA YOU DO.` · `TAPAS: THE HEAT OF EFFORT.` · `SVADHYAYA AND SURRENDER.` · then, large: `THINNING THE AFFLICTIONS.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Let's try all three, in miniature. Discipline: sit still, even when the body wants to shift, for just these few breaths. Study: notice one thing about your mind right now, honestly, as if reading a page. Restless? Tired? Calm? Surrender: offer this sit, whatever it's like, to something greater, God if you pray, or simply let go of needing it to be good. Then rest on the breath. The bell holds the time.
Kriya yoga. The yoga of action in sutra 2.1: discipline, study and surrender to the Lord, practiced to cultivate absorption and thin the afflictions.
Your line: three. Today, do one small thing from each: a bit of discipline, a page of study, and one action offered without needing credit for it. Day four hundred forty-seven.

448.hook: one short sutra names the five roots of human trouble, in the order they grow
448.tomorrow: ignorance — mistaking the passing for the permanent
448.howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras learn the five kleshas as the root diagnosis of suffering, and some teachers ask them to trace everyday reactions back to these roots during meditation and daily life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kriya yoga, three. Discipline, study, surrender, to cultivate absorption and thin the afflictions. Did you try one of each? Today, what exactly gets thinned. And the week closes. Day four hundred forty-eight.

A doctor can treat a fever, or find the infection causing it. It's easy to spend a life treating fevers: a flash of anger here, a craving there, a wave of fear at 2am. Patanjali goes looking for the infection. Yesterday he said kriya yoga thins the afflictions. Today, in sutra 2.3, he names them. There are five, and the commentators read the order as a line of growth, each one coming out of the one before, like branches from a trunk.
screen: `TREATING THE FEVER.` → `FINDING THE INFECTION.` → `FIVE ROOTS, IN ORDER.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.3: avidya asmita raga dvesha abhiniveshah kleshah. Ignorance, I-ness, attraction, aversion and clinging to life are the afflictions. Klesha means affliction, a trouble, something that causes pain. Here's the order, quickly, because each gets its own day this week. Avidya, ignorance: not a lack of facts, but seeing wrongly, taking what passes for what lasts. Asmita, I-ness: the sense of a separate me that grows out of that mistake. Raga, attraction: the pull toward what pleased that me. Dvesha, aversion: the push away from what hurt it. Abhinivesha: clinging to life, the deep fear of ending, which Patanjali says is found even in the wise. The commentators read it as a family tree. Misreading reality produces a small, separate self. A separate self wants things and fears things. And underneath all the wanting and fearing runs the will to keep going at any cost. Notice what isn't on the list: no demons, no sins, no bad luck. Just five ways the mind gets reality wrong and then defends the mistake. Now the week, from the top. Day one, many doors. Day two, mastery from the smallest to the largest. Day three, the crystal takes the color. Day four, truth-bearing wisdom. Day five, seedless, the end of chapter one. Day six, kriya yoga, chapter two begins. Today, the five afflictions, the roots that the whole practice is meant to thin.
screen: `KLESHA: AN AFFLICTION.` · `IGNORANCE, THEN I-NESS.` · `ATTRACTION, AVERSION, CLINGING.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `FIVE ROOTS, ONE FAMILY TREE.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle on the breath. As thoughts come, try sorting them into the five, gently, without fuss. A thought about wanting something: attraction. A thought about avoiding something: aversion. A thought that's all about me, my image, my place: I-ness. A flicker of fear about the future: clinging. You don't need to find ignorance; it's said to be under all of them. Just notice, name, and return. The bell holds the time.

Avidya, ignorance, mistaking the passing for the lasting, the root of the five afflictions. Patanjali names it first, then I-ness, attraction, aversion and clinging to life, each growing from the one before.
Your line: kleshas. The next time you feel a strong reaction today, ask which of the five it grows from before you act on it. Day four hundred forty-eight.

fork.setup: you snap at a friend over something small. Patanjali would want you to look where?
options: at the root: which affliction it grows from, and beneath it, ignorance.
fork.reveal: 2.3 names five roots. a snap is often aversion, or wounded I-ness, and the next sutra says all of them grow from ignorance.

original.note: Sanskrit kleśa: affliction, a cause of pain. Patanjali names five in 2.3.

trapdoor: what you thought: an affliction is a bad thing that happens to you.
what it means: five ways the mind misreads reality and then defends the mistake.
what a scholar hears: Vyasa calls the kleshas the five kinds of viparyaya, error, linking them back to 1.8; the same diagnostic idea of kleshas also appears in Buddhist thought.
